'''Mill River Park''' is a [https://parkserve.tpl.org/mapping/#/?CityID=0973000 23-acre urban park] located in downtown [[Stamford, Connecticut]]. The park, which separates Downtown from the West Side, features a restored section of the Mill River, extensive landscaping, and various recreational amenities. It is the result of a long-term redevelopment project aimed at reclaiming green space and improving the ecological health of the area.<ref name="groundcontrol">{{cite web |title=MILL RIVER PARK & GREENWAY |url=https://www.groundcontrol.design/mill-river |website=Ground Control |access-date=2024-07-03}}</ref> The park's development began in 1998 with a preliminary study by Sasaki Associates, resulting in the Mill River Corridor Plan to reclaim 26 acres of green space in downtown Stamford.<ref name="millriver">{{cite web |title=History of Mill River Park & Playground |url=https://millriverpark.org/the-park/history-of-mill-river-park-playground/ |website=Mill River Park Collaborative |access-date=2024-07-03}}</ref> In 2000, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers endorsed the removal of the Mill River Dam to restore wetland habitat and improve public access to the river. The Mill River Park Collaborative, a non-profit organization, was founded in 2003 to lead the creation, growth, and operations of the new park.<ref name="millriver" />

The park officially opened to the public in May 2013, featuring the largest cherry tree grove in New England. Since then, it has continued to evolve with the addition of new amenities, including a carousel in 2017, an ice skating rink and fountain in 2018, and the Whittingham Discovery Center, an environmental education facility, in 2022.<ref name="millriver" /><ref name="groundcontrol" /> 

== History ==
The park's history began in 1998, when landscape architecture firm [[Sasaki (company)|Sasaki Associates]] was commissioned to draft a plan to reclaim the area along a segment of the [[Rippowam River]] known as Mill River as a [[public park]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=History of Mill River Park & Playground |url=https://millriverpark.org/the-park/history-of-mill-river-park-playground/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220407023300/https://millriverpark.org/the-park/history-of-mill-river-park-playground/ |archive-date=2022-04-07 |access-date=2022-07-24 |website=Mill River Park Collaborative |language=en-US}}</ref>

In July 2007, the city government of [[Stamford, Connecticut|Stamford]] released a master plan for the redevelopment of the area.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Mill River Park & Greenway Master Plan |url=https://issuu.com/niarhodesjackson/docs/mill_river_masterplan_final_111109 |access-date=2022-07-24 |website=issuu.com |publisher=City of Stamford |language=en}}</ref> The plan entailed three stages: the first stage, where the [[United States Army Corps of Engineers|U.S. Army Corps of Engineers]] would remove a [[dam]] along the river and decrease the river's [[floodplain]],<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|pages=20-21}} a second stage for the construction of programming elements and walkways,<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|pages=22-23}} and a third stage for additional amenities.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|pages=22-23}} The width of the Mill River was to be narrowed to less than half of its then-expanse,{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}} which would expand the park's area and provide space for more amenities. The master plan outlined the construction of a [[carousel]], fountain, [[ice rink]], and a network of trails connecting a greenway with the Kosciuszko, Southfield, and Scalzi parks. Removing the dam will also allow fish to swim up from Long Island Sound. As of 2007, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers had spent $800,000 on preliminary studies, planning, and design.<ref name="mill" />

In 2009, an $8 million restoration of the Mill River, $5 million of which was federally funded, began. It was followed by a second $12-million phase, which consisted primarily of installing infrastructure such as lighting, benches, and plantings.<ref name="gtime">{{cite news | title=New Mill River Park unveiled | url=http://www.greenwichtime.com/news/article/New-Mill-River-Park-unveiled-4484729.php | first=Elizabeth | last=Kim | work=Greenwich Time | date=May 2, 2013 | access-date=June 9, 2013}}</ref>

Mill River Park was expanded in an $8.5 million project, including $4 million in federal funding earmarked in 2007, with the city government financing the rest of the cost. The federal funding was to pay for removing the Mill River dam and dredging.<ref name="mill">{{cite news |last=Porstner |first=Donna |title=Stamford to get $7M from feds |work=[[The Advocate (Stamford)|Stamford Advocate]] |date=December 20, 2007 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/stamford-advocate-stamford-to-get-7m-fr/203581774/ |page=A4 |access-date=August 11, 2026 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>

As of 2013, the master plan for Mill River Park is projected to cost $60 million and to encompass 28 acres.<ref name="gtime" />{{Needs update|date=July 2022}}

12 acres of the Mill River Park opened in May 2013.<ref name="gtime" />

In 2017, the park inaugurated the indoor carousel, and the ice skating rink and fountain were added in 2018.<ref name=":0" />

The Whittingham Discovery Center, a building for educational programming described by the [[Stamford Advocate]] as "part museum, part-classroom, part community space", opened in June 2022.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Valle |first=Verónica Del |date=2022-06-13 |title=Take a sneak peek at Stamford’s new science ‘discovery center’ in Mill River Park |url=https://www.stamfordadvocate.com/news/article/Take-a-sneak-peek-at-Stamford-s-new-science-17235885.php |access-date=2022-07-24 |website=[[Stamford Advocate]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Notable flora and fauna==
The Mill River Park was formerly home to a grove of [[Cherry tree|cherry trees]], which were presented to the city on April 27, 1957, by Junzo Nojima, a native of Japan who had settled in the city in 1926, and in 1932 became the first Japanese man to own a restaurant in the state (K&J Three Decker Restaurant on Atlantic Street).{{Citation needed|date=February 2019}} Nojima gave the city 120 trees, and for three years he watered each one until they took root.{{Citation needed|date=February 2019}} He gave the city instructions on how to care for them, but when they were overlooked, he began tending the trees himself.{{Citation needed|date=February 2019}} On Arbor Day, April 27, 2007, the city celebrated the 50th anniversary of the gift with a ceremony at the park.<ref>{{cite news |last=Deka |first=Christina |date=2007-04-27 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/stamford-advocate-on-arbor-day-city-wil/203581616/ |title=On Arbor Day, city will honor deep roots |work=[[The Advocate (Stamford)|Stamford Advocate]] |page=A11 |access-date=2026-08-11 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> The cherry trees were removed in March 2009, as part of the renovations in the park's construction,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Racine |first=Claire K. |date=2019-03-18 |title=This day in Stamford history: Historic cherry trees come down |url=https://www.stamfordadvocate.com/local/article/This-day-in-Stamford-history-Historic-cherry-13689609.php |access-date=2022-07-24 |website=[[Stamford Advocate]] |language=en-US}}</ref> but seeds from a select few were transferred to a nursery, and were planted in the fall of 2012.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gordon |first=Maggie |date=2012-05-06 |title=Stamford celebrates cherry blossoms |url=https://www.stamfordadvocate.com/news/article/Stamford-celebrates-cherry-blossoms-3537040.php |access-date=2022-07-24 |website=[[Stamford Advocate]] |language=en-US}}</ref>
